news.title: Third Trump Cabinet Member Moves to Military Base Amid Iran Threats: Report
news.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved out of his Washington-area home and onto a military base following threats against his life from Iran, according to a new report. Bessent's relocation, first reported by The New York Times on Tuesday, comes as U.S. officials assess that Iranian efforts to target current and former American officials have reached a more advanced stage. Three people familiar with the matter told the Times that intelligence about threats against Bessent contributed to the assessment. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive information. Bessent is the third current Trump Cabinet member reported to have moved into military housing, following Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who live at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C. The Treasury secretary's move comes as he leads the Trump administration's economic pressure campaign against Iran, seeking to isolate the country financially through sanctions and restrictions on trade routes. A Treasury Department spokesperson told the Times that Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats" and remains committed to carrying out the administration's pressure campaign. Newsweek has contacted the Treasury Department and the White House for comment. Bessent's Move Follows Iranian Threats U.S. officials in recent weeks concluded that Iranian plotting against current and former American officials had reached a more advanced stage, according to the Times. Intelligence about threats against Bessent was among the information contributing to that assessment. The severity of the threats against the Treasury secretary was not immediately clear. U.S. officials have said Iran's ability to carry out large-scale attacks in the United States and elsewhere overseas remains limited, even as they take specific threats against individuals seriously. Bessent has been a central figure in the administration's effort to weaken Iran's economy and cut off financial resources available to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Since August, the Treasury Department has pursued a campaign of tougher sanctions and restrictions on trade routes in an effort to isolate Tehran financially. The administration has argued that the measures are putting pressure on Iran's economy, weakening its currency and worsening living conditions. However, U.S. intelligence assessments have suggested that economic pressure alone may not persuade Iran's hard-line leadership to give up power. Officials have assessed that the country's leaders remain determined to retain control despite the economic consequences. Iran has previously been accused of plotting attacks against American officials. In 2024, federal prosecutors charged Farhad Shakeri, whom they described as an operative of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, in an alleged plot to kill President Donald Trump. The alleged effort was described by prosecutors as retaliation for the 2020 U.S. drone strike that killed Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani. Iranian threats have also targeted other people involved in that operation. Other Trump Officials Have Relocated Bessent is not the first senior Trump administration official to leave a private residence for military housing or other protected accommodations amid security concerns. Rubio and Hegseth have been living on Generals' Row at Fort McNair, a military installation in Washington that traditionally houses senior military officers. Their moves were reported last year, as several administration officials sought more secure accommodations. Kristi Noem, then the homeland security secretary, also moved into military housing at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling in Washington. She took up residence in a home typically designated for the Coast Guard commandant after the location of her Washington apartment building was publicized. White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and his family also moved into military housing after facing protests and security concerns outside their Arlington, Virginia, home. The move followed incidents involving protesters near the property and the publication of the family's address. Miller's relocation was not reported as being prompted by Iranian threats. The circumstances surrounding the various officials' moves have differed, with some linked to protests, the disclosure of home addresses or other security concerns. The Atlantic reported in October 2025 that at least six senior political appointees were living in Washington-area military housing. The publication also noted that the influx of civilian officials was putting pressure on housing traditionally reserved for senior military personnel. US Raises Alert Over Iranian Activity The reported move comes amid broader concerns among U.S. officials about Iranian efforts to target Americans. Last month, the administration placed some U.S. personnel in the Middle East on heightened alert and reduced staffing at certain embassies and consulates amid intelligence indicating that Iran was further along in planning attacks against Americans. The U.S. military also moved bombers from a base in the United Kingdom following concerns about a suspected terrorist plot, according to the Times. Iran's alleged efforts to target American officials have been a concern for successive administrations. The threat has been particularly pronounced for people associated with the 2020 killing of Soleimani, which Tehran vowed to avenge. The Biden administration maintained security details for some officials who faced threats related to the strike. Trump revoked protections for some former advisers shortly after returning to office. The latest reported relocation underscores the security concerns facing senior members of the administration as Washington continues its confrontation with Tehran. It remains unclear how long Bessent is expected to stay in military housing or whether officials anticipate further changes to his security arrangements. news.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has reportedly moved to a military base after threats against his life from Iran.
news.author: Steven Frank

news.title: Donald Trump lashes out at Republican 'loser' in tantrum over Hegseth impeachment attempt
news.text: US President Donald Trump has lashed out at Democrats, and a member of his own Republican Party, after an attempt to impeach his defence chief. The impeachment attempt comes after a major loss for Mr Trump. Republicans lost both the House and the Senate to Democrats last week in the midterm elections as voters made their opposition Mr Trump - and effectively Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's - war known. Mr Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday: "The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED! "Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete." Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky on Monday moved to force a vote to impeach Mr Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war, but his motion proved unsuccessful the following day. Republicans in the House blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Mr Hegseth, but he is not yet safe. Democrats will take control of Congress next year and possibly try again. Democrats sang support for impeachment articles. The articles accuse the defense secretary of the "high crimes and misdemeanors" of illegally ordering the military to wage war ⁠in Iran and Yemen, attack boats in the Caribbean Sea, and capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro at the start of the year, Reuters reports. The elections last week highlighted American dissatisfaction over the eight-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices and impacted the US economy as well as global markets. Mr Hegseth has been one of the administration's most prominent defenders of the war. Critics have long said the war was launched without proper authorization, but now Mr Hegseth has come under renewed fire. Mr Trump's rant continued: "Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot. "The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped! MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN. President DONALD J. TRUMP"
news.summary: The impeachment attempt comes after a major loss for the Republican Party last week, and although Pete Hegseth was saved from impeachment on Tuesday, attempts may be made again in January

news.title: Treasury's Bessent moved to military base after Iranian threats
news.text:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, an architect of President Donald Trump’s plan to inflict economic pain on Iran, has moved to a U.S. military base following death threats, The New York Times and Fox News reported Nov. 10.

Treasury department officials confirmed the move and said Bessent will "not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats," the Times and Fox reported. The severity of the threats wasn’t immediately clear.

USA TODAY has reached out to the Treasury Department and the White House for further information. The location of the base was not included in the reports.

Bessent’s reported move comes about nine months after the launch of the war that Trump has argued was necessary to ensure Iran did not obtain a nuclear weapon. Critics of the war have derided that justification for the on-again, off-again fighting, which has lasted far longer than the president said it would and inflicted a heavy economic toll on Americans.

Pentagon officials told Congress at the end of October that the war has thus far cost over $47 billion. Iran’s move to close the Strait of Hormuz also has caused gas prices to skyrocket and the war has taken a significant toll on the military’s stockpile of missiles, according to experts. 

In recent months, top U.S. officials have expressed concerns that Iran is switching up its tactics in order to potentially strike Americans outside the region. The United States hastily moved bombers out of Britain in early October amid a suspected terror plot at a base where the military staged flights to Iran.

Bessent’s move follows an announcement by FBI Director Kash Patel earlier on Nov. 10 that the Department of Justice had indicted three Iranian-backed operatives suspected of being behind nearly 20 plots across the United States and Europe.

According to the DOJ, the trio attempted to stage attacks on Jewish communities in the United States and Britain and were also involved in the suspected plot at the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain, where American service members were stationed. 

The Treasury secretary is the latest top Trump official to move onto a military base amid suspected threats. 

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth are neighbors on a military base in Washington, DC, Rubio previously said on a podcast. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem also lived on a Washington-area base towards the end of her tenure, USA TODAY Network member Nashville Tennessean previously reported. 

Top Trump aide and now White House chief of staff Stephen Miller moved onto military housing in September 2025 after facing what he described as harassment at his home in Virginia, The Atlantic reported. Miller is the chief architect of Trump’s unpopular and deadly mass deportations campaign. 

It’s unclear how much the move to federal housing for top White House officials is costing taxpayers.

news.title: World leaders begin talks at UN climate conference amid concerns that actions are inadequate, slow
news.text: Antalya World leaders will begin formal discussions Wednesday at the United Nations climate change conference in Turkiye, hoping to agree on concrete actions to curb global warming after a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other climate-related disasters. But what can and will be accomplished at the Conference of the Parties, called COP31, remains to be seen. Past talks have been criticised for making promises that later fell flat. While delegates at the 2023 conference in Dubai agreed to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas - the leading contributor to climate change - subsequent conferences in Azerbaijan and Brazil ended with little agreement on reductions. Last year's Brazil conference produced a compromise agreement pledging additional money to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate change. This year's conference - Turkiye is hosting and Australia is leading negotiations - officially kicked off Monday amid fears that the world is not moving quickly enough. Scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s. Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal set during the 2015 Paris Agreement and has been a focus of international negotiations. The talks also come as the war in Iran has increased global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. That has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar. “We don't need more promises, we need plans,” said John Kerry, former U.S. secretary of state and former presidential climate envoy, though the U.S. itself, the world's second-largest polluter after China, is noticeably absent for the second year in a row. US President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.
news.summary: Scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s

news.title: Father and son among seven killed by Israeli fire in Gaza Strip
news.text:
RAMALLAH/GENEVA: Israeli forces killed at least seven Pales-tinians, including a father and his 13-year-old son, in the Gaza Strip on Tuesday, local health officials said.

Medics said Fadi Rajab and his son Abubakr were killed in an airstrike that hit the roof of a displacement shelter in the Zeitoun neighbourhood in Gaza City. A third Palestinian was killed in an Israeli airstrike near a school in Gaza City’s Daraj neighbourhood, health officials added.

In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, Israeli gunfire killed a man, medics said. Later on Tuesday, an Israeli airstrike hit a metal foundry in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City, killing three people, medics said, taking the day’s death toll to at least seven.

Israeli forces shot dead a 14-year-old in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials said, with Israel saying it was responding to stone-throwing.

Moutaz Eyad Daghlas was killed in Burqa, northwest of Nablus, late on Monday, the Palestinian health ministry said.

Unicef says Tel Aviv blocks Gaza basin repairs, warns of flood risk

The Palestine Red Crescent Society said its teams treated two people with gunshot wounds and took them to hospital, but that Israeli forces blocked access to a third wounded person and detained three volunteer paramedics.

Israeli forces have routinely opened live fire on Palestinians including minors who throw stones in the West Bank, which Israel has controlled since 1967.

The Israeli human rights group B’Tselem said Israeli forces killed at least 241 children or teenagers in the territory between the Oct 7, 2023 raid by Hamas and late June this year.

Violence has increased in recent weeks, especially in the run-up to Israel’s Oct 27 election, before which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had sought to appeal to hardline settlers in the West Bank.

On Oct 23, Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near Hebron before being killed by Israeli forces, who later responded with a major operation in the flashpoint city.

Flood risk in Gaza

The UN children’s agency said Israel had rejected the importation of equipment needed to repair a water basin in Gaza, and warned that the facility could overflow and endanger nearby residents through flooding and disease.

Local authorities say Israel destroyed water infrastructure and vehicles used to pump water during its war against Hamas, which had displaced most of the territory’s more than two million residents and left much of Gaza in ruins. Most of the population now lives in tent camps.

One damaged facility is the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin in Gaza City, which is now contaminated with sewage and at risk of overflowing after heavy rainfall, according to Unicef’s James Elder.

He told reporters the agency had been working with Israeli authorities and US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace for a year on a $3 million plan to repair it, but that COGAT, the Israeli military agency overseeing humanitarian affairs in Gaza, had rejected the project in the past few days.

“Toxic sewage could flow into the streets and tents of Gaza City, forcing children and families from their makeshift homes once more, and grossly increasing the threat of disease. So we’re a bit baffled,” he told a press briefing in Geneva. “Let’s do the rehabilitation before this becomes another entirely preventable killer of girls and boys in Gaza,” he said.

This week, heavy rain has already flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians crammed into encampments across the Gaza Strip. Four people, including three small children, were killed when a sand embankment collapsed on their tents in an incident that highlighted the risks ahead of the rainy winter season.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops.

World Health Organisation spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said at the same briefing there were significant communicable disease risks in Gaza due to flooding, poor sanitation and insufficient health and water services. Nearly 1 million displaced people across Gaza now faced medium or high flood risk, he said.

news.title: US fails to show for UN rights review, yet again
news.text:
GENEVA: The United States boycotted on Tuesday a United Nations review of its human rights record for a second time, in an unprecedented snub of a process that all countries traditionally submit to. US seats were left empty at the world body’s European headquarters in Geneva for the so-called Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which all 193 UN member states undergo every four to five years.

As the review was set to begin, UN Human Rights Council president Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro, of Indonesia, looked at the empty seats behind the US nameplate and said that “the delegation of the United States is not present in the room”.

The US absence was not a surprise. President Donald Trump’s administration decided shortly after his return to power in January 2025 to halt cooperation with the rights council, and had already boycotted the UPR process last November.

In response, the council at the time had postponed the US review for a year, in the hope that Washington would return. The US State Department said this week that the administration considers the council an “irredeemable body” that “makes a mockery of human rights”, suggesting that it would not participate in any of its mechanisms, including the UPR.

‘Accountability is important’

Despite the continued boycott, rights advocates, civil society organisations and US elected officials have gathered in Geneva this week to keep a spotlight on alleged US rights abuses. Among them was Noor Abdalla, the wife of Mahmoud Khalil, the prominent pro-Palestinian protest leader and green card holder whom the Trump administration sought to deport last year. “Accountability is important,” she told reporters.

“When the most powerful government in the world is not held acc-o--untable, they think that they can do whatever they want to do… We saw that with my husband’s case.” Washington’s complete non-compliance with the process is unprecedented. Before the United States, only Israel had previously boycotted its UPR, in early 2013, although it underwent a delayed review later that year. Some countries have sought postponements since the UPR process began in 2008, while Nicaragua partially boycotted the process, but only after its latest review had already taken place.

‘Hypocrisy’

Several diplomats spoke up on Tuesday about the value of the UPR, with the European Union representative saying Brussels “regrets any situation in which full engagement… does not occur, including the decision by the United States again not to participate”. Cuban ambassador Rodolfo Benitez Verson voiced outrage at Washington’s absence.

“The United States is the only country in the history of the Human Rights Council which has refused to take part in the UPR cycle without even presenting its national report,” he told the council, slamming US “double standards and hypocrisy”.

Published in Dawn, November 11th, 2026

news.title: Biographer says Trump aware voters find him 'incompetent and loathsome'
news.text:
As the curtain opens to the second half of President Donald Trump’s term, Trump’s biographer expects Trump to do nothing useful or meaningful other than dance for cameras and struggle to remain relevant.

An ugly battle is underway in Trump’s head, said biographer Michael Wolff, speaking on the "Trump's Brain" podcast with Joanna Coles. A media-dependent psychopath, who had convinced himself that the world loves him without question is suddenly now having to deal with nationwide humiliation and unquestionable rejection. And things are getting ugly fast behind his eyes.

“Trump now has this thing that has happened, an existential moment in his presidency and in his political career: Broad repudiation from every almost every aspect of the country and from his own party,” said Wolff. “It’s a kind of national waking up and saying ‘this guy is incompetent and loathsome and doesn't deliver on anything.’ So now he's got two more years in office. How does he react to that?”

While Wolff said saner presidents resort to the “politically tried and true method” of compromise, by admitting their defeat and targeting the reasons for that defeat, that’s not going to happen here.

“Remember in a traditional presidency you really are looking for the things that you can now accomplish with the opposition in charge. Accomplishment, when you're the president, is usually measured in legislation that you can pass,” said Wolff. “But that's not something that Trump is interested in. That's not a measure that he acknowledges or accepts. So what is the measure? Well, the measure for Trump is the attention he receives and the persona he maintains.”

According to Wolff, Trump’s only goal all his life was to “always be a Donald Trump that is bigger and greater than ever before.” But, of course, this is a problem now in his newly diminished capacity with Democrats socking his policies and burying him in investigations over allegations of corruption and self-enrichment. That won’t stop him from trying to inflate himself, of course. Nothing ever does.

“I'm absolutely positive this not really a reversion, but an increase of this persona of ‘I am implacable. I give back always harder than I get. I am the UFC champion,” said Wolff.

Wolff said under these circumstances, with a president focused singularly upon himself to the cost of all else, the next American president can expect Trump's Iran mess to be waiting for him at his door step.

news.title: Hegseth has survived an attempt to oust him – for now. A much bigger fight looms
news.text:
As a historic “blue wave” swept the Democrats to victory in last week’s US midterms, the likely incoming House oversight committee chair, Democratic lawmaker Robert Garcia, had a simple message for US President Donald Trump and his allies: “Lawyer up”.

But before the new Democrat-controlled Congress has even been sworn in, it’s a member of Trump’s own party who has caused the latest headache for his administration.

On Monday, outgoing Kentucky Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, took to the House floor to formally introduce a 34-page impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense. 

Albeit an extraordinary rebuke, the move was unlikely to succeed, with Republicans still in power until January.

And indeed, on Tuesday, the Republican-led House voted 211-204 to refer it to committee, effectively killing off the measure for the remainder of this Congress. Hegseth has survived this attempt to oust him.

Any reprieve, however, may be short-lived. With the Democrats preparing to take control of Congress, how does impeachment of a cabinet official work? And could Hegseth still become the first US defence secretary in history to be removed from office?

What is impeachment?

Nearly 240 years ago, the framers of the US Constitution, fearful of tyranny, wanted a legislative process that could check abuses of executive power and remove a president or official who committed them.

Article II, Section 4 of the Constitution reads:

The President, Vice President and all civil Officers of the United States, shall be removed from Office on Impeachment for, and Conviction of, Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors.

The Constitution vests the House with “the sole Power of Impeachment”, which takes only a simple majority. 

But impeachment only represents the formal process of laying charges. Removal from office is a much taller order, and requires a conviction through a trial in the Senate, with a two-thirds supermajority. 

In other words, 67 of the 100 senators must vote to convict for the individual to be removed.

Not an ordinary courtroom

Unlike standard criminal or civil court proceedings with strict burdens of proof, the grounds for impeachment remain vague. 

US Founding Father Alexander Hamilton characterised impeachable offences as those stemming from “the misconduct of public men, or in other words, from the abuse or violation of some public trust”.

Ultimately, as one academic put it: 

Impeachment is a political process, albeit with legal overtones.

And while it’s been back in the spotlight in the Trump era, impeachment is still exceptionally rare — especially for cabinet officials. Only two US cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached, and neither was ultimately convicted and removed from office.

In 2024, during the Biden administration, US Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by House Republicans over enforcement of immigration policy.

Then-President Joe Biden denounced the vote, which fell on party lines, as “baseless”.

The only other case occurred back in the Gilded Age. In 1876, the House voted unanimously to impeach US Secretary of War William Belknap over corruption allegations, despite the fact that Belknap had resigned from office just a few hours before. 

What were the allegations against Hegseth?

Massie’s resolution contained eight articles of impeachment, which claimed Hegseth has abused his powers through unlawful acts – “especially with regard to the commission of war”.

Most articles accuse Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval. Among the most notable examples, it cites the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro back in January, and the launch of military action against Iran less than two months later. 

Massie is a long-term and outspoken libertarian critic of Trump. 

After being toppled by a Trump-endorsed primary challenger earlier this year, he will no longer represent Kentucky’s fourth congressional district in the incoming Congress. 

With little to lose, and in the final months of a Republican-controlled Congress, Massie said he was “doing this because it’s the right thing to do”.

The political price of war

But the timing also reflects the political fallout from the Iran war, which many Republicans have blamed for their devastating rout at the midterms. 

In recent months, survey after survey has found the vast majority of Americans disapprove of the government’s handling of the conflict and are concerned about higher gas and fuel prices. 

A YouGov poll conducted on the eve of the midterm elections found a candidate’s support for the Iran war was more than three times as likely to put voters off as win them over. 

It wouldn’t be the first time an unpopular war has cost a Pentagon official their job. In 2006, President George W Bush announced Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s resignation the day after Democrats won back Congress in a bruising midterm defeat for the Republicans.

This had been largely driven by public discontent with the Iraq war.

Against this backdrop, Massie was likely betting that the midterm result has given Republican lawmakers – including some 70 House representatives who will be vacating their seats in January – a renewed willingness to flex their legislative muscles in the twilight of this Congress.

Controlling the fall

Massie has argued that Hegseth’s removal from office could provide Republicans the opportunity to confirm a replacement before the Democratic Party takes over both chambers. This, he has said, would be:

a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year.

Chances are, he’s right. Expected incoming Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries has previously signalled that targeting the high-profile cabinet official would be top of the party’s to-do list in a Democratic-controlled Congress: 

One of the first things we’re going to do in the majority, we’re going to run Pete Hegseth out of town.

Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, Jeffries declared himself a “hard yes” on Massie’s resolution and anticipated it would enjoy “incredibly strong support” from his party colleagues. 

Why conviction remains unlikely

Democrats could be primed to mount their own similar case against Hegseth when they take control of the chamber in January.

However, even if next year an impeachment resolution can sail through the new Democratic-majority House, it is still unlikely to clear the high two-thirds bar in the Senate required for conviction. For his part, Trump has vowed to “stand by” Hegseth.

But Hegseth may still end up leaving office, one way or another. As one researcher predicted before the midterms, any impeachments of cabinet officers that proceed to trial with even modest Republican support could force those officials to resign.

Whatever happens, this ordeal is a first taste of what’s to come for the Trump administration over the next two years. And the Democrats barely had to lift a finger.

news.title: US extends 178 China tariff exclusions to January 9
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 11 (IANS) The United States has extended exemptions from additional tariffs on 178 categories of Chinese goods until January 9, 2027, as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over trade commitments. The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Tuesday (local time) announced the two-month extension in a Federal Register notice published Tuesday, preventing the exclusions from expiring after November 9. The decision allows American importers to continue bringing in specified Chinese products without paying the additional duties imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The extension covers goods entering the United States from November 10, 2026, until 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027. "In light of ongoing discussions with China, the Trade Representative has determined that it is appropriate to further extend all 178 current exclusions until January 10, 2027," the notice said. The exclusions cover 164 product categories carried forward from earlier tariff relief measures and 14 categories involving equipment used in solar manufacturing. They apply only to products meeting specific customs classifications and descriptions. Other Chinese imports remain subject to applicable tariffs. USTR said it considered public comments received during previous reviews, recommendations from advisory committees and advice from the interagency Section 301 Committee before granting the extension. The agency also left open the possibility of further changes. "The Trade Representative may continue to consider further extensions or additional modifications as appropriate," the notice said. The announcement comes four days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held a videoconference with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on November 6. During the discussion, Greer pressed Beijing to fulfil commitments made under earlier trade agreements, particularly those involving American agricultural exports, rare earth elements and other critical minerals. Greer emphasised the importance of China taking concrete steps to implement those commitments. The administration said it would continue monitoring compliance while pursuing a more balanced trading relationship that benefits American farmers, manufacturers and workers. The extension, among other things, builds on a trade understanding reached between President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in November 2025. Under that arrangement, Washington agreed to maintain exclusions from certain additional tariffs, while Beijing committed to extending its own exclusions on American goods through December 31, 2026. The agreement addressed Chinese purchases of US agricultural products, restrictions on rare earth exports and trade measures affecting American semiconductor companies. USTR subsequently extended the 178 exclusions through November 9, 2026. Tuesday's decision provides another two months for businesses relying on the exemptions. The agency said US Customs and Border Protection would issue instructions governing customs entries and implementation of the extension.

news.title: World leaders begin talks at UN climate conference amid concerns that actions are inadequate, slow
news.text: World leaders will begin formal discussions Wednesday at the United Nations climate change conference in Turkey, hoping to agree on concrete actions to curb global warming after a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other climate-related disasters.But what can and will be accomplished at the Conference of the Parties, called COP31, remains to be seen. Past talks have been criticized for making promises that later fell flat.While delegates at the 2023 conference in Dubai agreed to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas — the leading contributor to climate change — subsequent conferences in Azerbaijan and Brazil ended with little agreement on reductions. Last year's Brazil conference produced a compromise agreement pledging additional money to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate change.This year's conference — Turkey is hosting and Australia is leading negotiations — officially kicked off Monday amid fears that the world is not moving quickly enough.Scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial levels of the early 1800s. Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal set during the 2015 Paris Agreement and has been a focus of international negotiations..Greta Thunberg warns 'everything we love is at stake' as she arrives at UN climate talks.The talks also come as the war in Iran has increased global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. That has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.“We don’t need more promises, we need plans,” said John Kerry, former US secretary of state and former presidential climate envoy, though the U.S. itself, the world’s second-largest polluter after China, is noticeably absent for the second year in a row.US President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions..India stresses equity in global climate action at COP31; says no one should be left behind.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: ‘De-risk, not decouple’: Bessent says US-China must cooperate on AI risks
news.text: The United States and China must work together to manage the risks posed by advanced artificial intelligence while recognising that their competition for technological leadership will continue, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday.Bessent said the two countries should not underestimate their differences as they prepare to establish a new dialogue on “superintelligence” during US President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen next week.The meeting, scheduled on the sidelines of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit, will be Trump’s third meeting with Xi this year. Bessent, who is due to travel to China for the talks, said Washington wanted to build a relationship with Beijing based on “balance and reciprocity”.“As SI advances, so will the need to engage in new areas of risk management — and to demonstrate how two nations can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership,” Bessent said in prepared remarks to the National Committee on US-China Relations in New York.He added that the two sides should “harbour no illusions about the differences between the United States and China”, noting that their interests and approaches would not always align.US and China plan dialogue on superintelligence risksThe proposed dialogue on superintelligence, or SI, is intended to help Washington and Beijing address shared risks and avoid misunderstandings between their respective systems, Bessent said.The discussions are expected to cover the evaluation and testing of advanced AI models before their release, as well as measures to ensure that human judgement remains in control of the technology.“We also expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment firmly in command of this technology,” he said.The two countries have also agreed to establish a direct communication channel to alert each other about serious incidents involving the technology.Trump and Xi agreed on the AI alert system during their previous meeting at the White House in September. However, Trump had then expressed reluctance to introduce additional safeguards, saying he wanted to protect US leadership in the field, Reuters reported.Bessent outlines trade initiatives ahead of Trump-Xi meetingBessent also referred to trade agreements reached during the two previous Trump-Xi meetings, including plans for a “Board of Trade” to determine reciprocal tariff reductions on $30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods in each direction.China has also pledged to purchase US agricultural products, he said.A proposed “Board of Investment” would provide a structured forum to discuss market access for American companies operating in China and offer greater predictability for Chinese businesses, Bessent added.He acknowledged that the US trade deficit with China remained a point of friction but reiterated that Washington's objective was to reduce risks in the economic relationship rather than sever trade ties.“The US objective is to ‘de-risk, not to decouple’ from trade with China,” he said.Bessent invoked the first US trade voyage to China in 1784, when American merchants exchanged ginseng for Chinese tea, porcelain and silk, to underline the importance of maintaining areas of cooperation despite competing interests.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces shareholder lawsuitBessent did not refer in his remarks to the controversy surrounding Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who is facing an internal investigation by the company's board over reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence services of having links to Chinese intelligence.China's foreign ministry has dismissed the espionage allegations as “groundless” and “a smear”. Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe that US national security or the company's secrets were compromised, while Jensen Huang has pledged to cooperate with the internal review.The controversy has also prompted a shareholder lawsuit against Nvidia and its chief executive.According to news agency AP, retail investor Mark Kistenmacher filed a complaint in a California court on Monday, accusing the company and Huang of misleading investors about the relationship and its potential implications for national security and Nvidia's business.The complaint alleges that Nvidia failed to disclose Huang's relationship with Alice Huang and made misleading statements about its dealings with her company, Singapore-based Megaspeed International. The company had earlier said its compliance team had checked Megaspeed's activities and found no evidence of wrongdoing, AP reported.The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and a jury trial on behalf of investors who purchased Nvidia shares between October 9, 2025, and November 8, 2026.Nvidia's independent directors said on Tuesday that they had appointed the New York-based law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent investigation” into the matter. Joon H. Kim, a partner at the firm and a former acting US attorney for the Southern District of New York, will lead the inquiry.Trump said on Monday that the FBI was investigating the affair. He also said Huang had told him that he had no idea the woman could be involved in espionage, adding that he did not think the Nvidia chief had reason to worry.Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping out around $190 billion in market value, and declined a further 5.5% by Tuesday's close.Huang has acknowledged the affair and apologised to his wife, family and the company in an open letter published on Nvidia's website.“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent highlighted the importance of cooperation in managing artificial intelligence risks. The discussion aims to address shared technological challenges and ensure human oversight remains paramount. Trade agreements have also been outlined to strengthen economic ties between the two nations.

news.text:
ANTALYA: World leaders will set out their climate priorities in speeches at COP31 in ​Turkiye on Wednesday, as negotiators seek agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy ‌use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention.

A UN report last month found the world on course to ​break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to ​prevent the worst of climate change.

Former French Prime Minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris ⁠climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said the speeches could give political impetus to the negotiations.

“It is an ​opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya ​is implementation,” he told Reuters.

Scores of world leaders – including presidents and heads of government – will begin their rapid-fire speeches on Wednesday afternoon and continue through the day on Thursday, according to the COP31 schedule.

Wednesday’s speakers are expected to include Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who was re-elected at the end of ​October, and whose country hosted last year’s climate talks.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and Marshall Islands ​President Hilda Heine will also speak on Wednesday.

The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, has skipped the talks for the second year in a ‌row after ⁠President Donald Trump – who has called global warming a hoax – withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025.

Age of electricity?

COP31 host Turkiye has so far been pushing the government representatives attending the conference to put a goal on electrification at the centre of a final deal, even as critics say it may do little to curb warming.

The proposal targets a rise in electricity’s share of total ​global energy consumption to 35% by ​2035, up from a little ⁠over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories, and buildings.

But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and world governments have yet ​to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

“It ​is long past ⁠time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told the conference on Tuesday, urging countries to produce clear timelines for the transition.

The previous COP in Brazil was unable to reach consensus on the need for a global plan ⁠to reduce ​dependency on fossil fuels.

The Brazilian COP presidency has in recent weeks, however, published a roadmap ​aimed at keeping that idea central to the climate negotiations. It asks countries to first plan and assess their energy systems by 2028, then work together to reduce ​fossil fuel supply from 2031.

news.title: Nvidia CEO affair revives push for tougher US line on China
news.text:
WASHINGTON, United States: The scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang could have its biggest consequences in Washington, where China hawks are seizing on the affair to push a hard line that had been put on the back burner under President Donald Trump.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world’s leading supplier of the processors that power artificial intelligence, admitted on Sunday to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US intelligence officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence.

Trump, who has relied on Huang as an adviser on AI, called him “an honorable guy” and said Huang told him he had no idea the woman was a spy.

Huang has spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced AI chips to China, and Trump last year cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there over objections from hawks in both parties.

“China hawks in policy circles in Washington DC were quite frustrated with the decisions and really wanted to see a more aggressive approach around export controls to China,” said Aalok Mehta of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“They will now see some fruits of their efforts.”

Many in Washington see the United States as locked in a Cold War-style race with China for technological and military dominance, and these hawks have bristled at Trump not conforming to that.

“What we are heading into is one of the most serious investigative efforts in a substantial period,” said Kurt Campbell, a former US deputy secretary of state and co-founder of consultancy The Asia Group.

Lawmakers will want to know when the government learned of the alleged links, whether the president was warned and whether the contacts shaped his China policy, Campbell said.

The New York Times has reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the allegations to Trump in May, but the president chose not to act.

Nvidia committed $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom — among the largest donations — months after securing his approval to resume chip sales to China, The Washington Post reported. Nvidia has said the gift was independent of its business interests.

Three Republican House committee chairs have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his dealings with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against espionage.

Not ‘invincible’ 

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, said Republicans long feared crossing Trump.

But with the party having lost control of Congress and Trump “no longer this seemingly invincible political brand,” some may feel freer to break with him, Chan told AFP.

That could revive the AI Overwatch Act, a bipartisan bill that would let Congress review and block licenses to export advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.

The revelations have given hawks “new enthusiasm” to push through the stalled annual defense authorization bill with export control measures attached, said Emily Benson, head of strategy at Minerva Technology Futures.

The key question is Trump, she said, who holds a veto that only two-thirds majorities in both chambers can override.

Commerce Department staff have also pushed for new rules, including curbs on Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will not act without Trump’s instruction, tech news outlet The Information reported.

The department has already drawn scrutiny for reportedly halting a probe into Megaspeed’s dealings with Nvidia.

Tighter rules risk upsetting the trade truce Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping reached last year.

Export control legislation seen by Beijing as targeting China “would almost certainly invite swift retaliatory action by Beijing to destabilize US supply chains,” Benson said.

The FBI is looking into the spying allegations, Trump said, while the Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia chips into China, NBC News reported.

Megaspeed denies smuggling, and Beijing has dismissed the spying claims as smears.

If wrongdoing were found and Huang forced out, “that would have huge implications for AI in the US, given that he has played such a pivotal role in pushing forward Nvidia but also the whole industry,” Chan said.

But even short of Huang’s downfall, “Nvidia’s traction within the halls of Congress and within the administration is likely to be significantly reduced or completely eliminated,” Mehta said.
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admitted affair is prompting China hawks in Washington to advocate for a stricter US approach to China. The incident follows a period of softened policies from the Trump administration.

news.title: 'Nobody’s paying attention' — and not even Trump’s 'mayhem' can save him
news.text:

Now that he suffered a devastating political blow with Republican losses in the 2026 midterm elections, Trump's behavior has become even more noticeably bizarre, especially as he causes "mayhem" because he fears "nobody's paying attention."

"Coping with loss looks different for everyone, and President Trump has processed the country’s nearly wholesale rejection of the Republican Party in the midterm elections in his own way," reported The New York Times' Katie Rogers on Tuesday.

"The last week has seen the president renew false claims about rigged elections, float a mixed martial arts executive as his new press secretary, muse about the beams in the White House ballroom, oust his chief of staff and call unannounced into C-SPAN," Rogers added.

As one example, Rogers noted how Trump seemed to cheapen the losses of the Russia-Ukraine War by comparing them to rally sizes.

“I just think that Ukraine and Russia are tired of fighting," Trump said per Rogers at his Tuesday press conference. "They’re tired of seeing dead young soldiers, mostly soldiers. Most of the people are soldiers. Think of it. They’re losing 25,000 — Dana, can you imagine 25,000? That’s like a stadium, Madison Square Garden. You have your fights, 25,000. That’s what it holds, and they’re losing that every single month, dead, young beautiful people, and it’s — it’s got to stop.”

On another occasion Trump rambled during a call to C-SPAN.

“Frankly, a big problem we had is the mental institutions being dumped into our country," Trump said when asked about the recent midterm election results. "Some very dangerous people were released into our country, to put it mildly. So we have not put the same, uh, pressure, obviously, and, you know, the, uh, we call them the worst of the worst. We haven’t put the same pressure on waitresses and, and on farm workers, et cetera. Not even close.”

Rogers is not alone in reporting that Trump's mental state has deteriorated since his losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

"In the days since his defeat, he has sounded like a man in denial," The New York Times' Peter Baker wrote on Sunday. "With his party still picking through the wreckage of a political earthquake, a seemingly oblivious President Trump signed a steel beam for his new White House ballroom and flew to Florida to give a speech on the space program. He seems flat these days, maybe a little dazed."

news.text:
Members of the Kennedy family have joined a lawsuit to block the building of US President Donald Trump's Independence Arch in Washington DC out of concern it might mar family gravesites.

The arch is part of Mr Trump's plan to leave his mark on the US capital, which so far has included renovations to the White House's east wing, the construction of a new golf course and work on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The arch is planned to be 76 metres tall and would also act as a "top-grade military complex", according to the president.

He said it would "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage".

The development has faced legal action, and now the children and grandchildren of Robert F Kennedy and Edward M Kennedy have lent their family's name to efforts challenging its construction.

The Democracy Defenders Fund, a group pursuing several legal challenges against Mr Trump's administration and representing the Kennedy family members leading the filing, said the arch could affect the nearby resting place of several family members as well as the John F Kennedy Eternal Flame.

In the filing, the complainants argued the arch's location on Memorial Circle in Washington DC would obstruct "a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the nation following the Civil War that has existed for nearly a century".

"That will also obstruct the clear sightline of the Kennedy Gravesites and JFK Eternal Flame in Arlington National Cemetery, from the Arlington Memorial Bridge, destroying an essential element of the Gravesites' design; and will permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country, including the Kennedy Gravesites," they said.

Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy, speaking on behalf of the family, said their legal action is about "protecting sacred spaces that belong to the American people".

"Our parents, Robert and Ethel Kennedy, and our uncles, President John F Kennedy and Senator Edward M Kennedy, are laid to rest at Arlington National Cemetery," they said.

"Our uncle Joseph P Kennedy Jr who lost his life serving our country in World War II, is also memorialised there."

Rory and Maxwell Kennedy were also among 15 Kennedy family members who endorsed Joe Biden's 2024 presidential campaign over Robert Kennedy Jr, who currently serves as Secretary of Health in Mr Trump's cabinet.

"A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come."

Former Obama administration ethics watchdog and Democracy Defenders Fund co-founder Norm Eisen called the "gigantic" proposed arch an illegal interference with the cemetery.

"Only Congress has the constitutional power to authorise an intrusion of this magnitude," Mr Eisen said.

"Today, members of the Kennedy family are joining with the other litigants in this case to protect this historic site, and to defend the rule of law and separation of powers."

The National Capital Planning Commission approved final site and building plans for the arch on November 5.

A judge has already issued a temporary order blocking construction through November 19 as she considers whether to issue a preliminary injunction, according to Reuters.

Numerous Democrats in Congress have vowed to block construction once they take control in January, after winning November's midterm elections.
news.summary: Nine members of the Kennedy family have joined a lawsuit to block the construction of the US president's Independence Arch.
news.author: Fergus Gregg

news.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, for now
news.text:
WASHINGTON, Nov 11 – An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives agreed to refer impeachment articles to a committee – essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky – for now.

In his first news briefing from the Pentagon in six months, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a “farce” and “sabotage”.

The bid to find the Cabinet Secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

Massie was the only Republican to vote against moving the resolution to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

His effort failed in a 211-204 vote, with more than a dozen members, including 11 Democrats, missing the vote.

The move to send the measure to the panel effectively kills the effort, as there is only a short period of time left in this Congress before Democrats take control in January.

President Trump celebrated the vote in a post on Truth Social, saying the effort “has miserably FAILED”.

“Again, Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” Trump said, referring to Hegseth.

Massie had previously acknowledged his impeachment bid may not succeed immediately, but argued it could help push Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process

news.title: US senators push tougher China AI chip curbs
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 11 (IANS) Senior US lawmakers from both parties are pressing for tighter controls on the export of advanced American artificial intelligence chips to China, warning that allegations involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang have heightened national security concerns. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday (local time) urged Congress to move quickly on three bipartisan bills designed to restrict China's access to American technology. His call followed a joint statement by Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and Republican Senator Jim Banks demanding stronger export controls. The renewed push comes as lawmakers consider including restrictions on advanced semiconductor technology in the annual defence policy legislation. Schumer called for passage of the AI OVERWATCH Act, the MATCH Act and the Chip Security Act, arguing that Washington must prevent sensitive American technology from reaching potential adversaries. He also demanded an immediate briefing for the Senate and House intelligence committees on alleged Chinese efforts to obtain information from Nvidia and other American AI companies. "We need a full accounting for Trump's failure to address foreign espionage in the American tech industry," Schumer said in remarks on the Senate floor. Schumer accused President Donald Trump of failing to adequately confront intelligence concerns. Warren and Banks, both members of the Senate Banking Committee, said they had urged the Commerce Department in March to reconsider Nvidia's export licences to China and conduct a comprehensive national security review. They alleged that Nvidia had subsequently received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies with reported connections to the Chinese military. The lawmakers said the latest allegations reinforced the need for stricter safeguards against the possible military use of American technology. "The Commerce Department should complement these efforts with immediate action to close export control loopholes," Warren and Banks said in their joint statement. Their appeal followed reports that Huang had been targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence operation involving a personal relationship. Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation on November 8 to examine whether its chief executive had been the target of foreign intelligence activity. The company said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, would oversee the investigation. China rejected the allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun described the accusations as groundless and an attempt to smear Beijing. Trump has publicly defended Huang, saying the Nvidia chief had told him he did not know the woman involved was suspected of espionage. The President said he believed Huang's explanation. The allegations remain under investigation, and no finding has established that Huang knowingly assisted Chinese intelligence or that company secrets were compromised.

Huang has told ​employees he was unfaithful to his wife, but provided no details about the relationship. The board has retained Joon Kim, a Wachtell Lipton partner and former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, whose practice includes internal investigations and white-collar defense, to lead the probe.Nvidia's stock, which had been nearly flat this year before news of the affair broke, has fallen 9.5% since then. news.title: Jets fans mercilessly boo 'coward' Connor Hellebuyck in return to Winnipeg
news.text:
Why did Connor Hellebuyck request trade from Jets?

Before Tuesday's game, Hellebuyck told the media his trade request became "very certain" after his family received threats. He didn't offer specifics but noted that not all of them were online.

"There were some moments and some things that happened to my family that, for me, crossed the line," he said (h/t Field Level Media). "I needed to be a good husband, a good father and do what's best for my family and career." 

Hellebuyck noted he "loved his time" in Winnipeg after playing for the Jets for 11 of his 12 NHL seasons. 

It's unclear if the threats were politically motivated. After helping Team USA win its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Winter Olympics, Hellebuyck was one of a handful of players to visit President Donald Trump at the White House. Trump awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. 

It's also worth noting Hellebuyck often wilted in the playoffs during his tenure with the Jets. The three-time Vezina Trophy winner's save percentage drops from .916 in the regular season to .903 in the playoffs. He posted a career-worst .866 save percentage during the 2025 Stanley Cup Playoffs. 

Regardless, the relationship between Winnipeg fans and Hellebuyck is only growing more frigid. Don't expect it to improve anytime soon.

news.title: Iran urges US to meet terms for Hormuz opening
news.text:
Araghchi says reopening proposal remains on table• Rubio sees no need for major combat operations as economic pressure continues• Qatar PM joins G7 talks after meeting Trump; US president sees ‘positive momentum’• Iran says three oil tankers on fire in Hormuz; October LNG traffic hits post-war high

TEHRAN: Iran on Tuesday urged the United States to accept its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, insisting that diplomacy rather than military action or further sanctions was the only way to end the war, as President Donald Trump saw “positive momentum” towards resolving the conflict.

The diplomatic push gained traction as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no need for major combat operations against Iran, while Qatar’s prime minister joined European and Saudi diplomats for talks on the crisis on the sidelines of a G7 meeting in Paris.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran’s proposal to reopen the strategic waterway within two days of an agreement with Washington remained on the table.

“The conflict with Iran will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions,” Araghchi told the official IRNA news agency.

“The only solution is to adopt a language of respect, engage in diplomacy and address Iran’s demands and conditions — which were outlined in the two-day proposal and remain on the table,” he added.

Iran’s conditions include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing its assets abroad, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

However, Washington insists that nuclear issues must feature in the initial negotiations.

Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei struck a more confrontational tone, urging Washington to “surrender” to Tehran’s demands.

“The war on Iran has already wrecked the US government. But Washington flails like a desperate gambler. FOLD YOUR HAND,” he posted on X.

US sees diplomatic progress

Speaking after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris, Rubio said Wash-ington’s economic pressure campaign had made further major attacks unnecessary.

“The economic campaign (against Iran) is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations,” he said. “That’s what I told our allies here today.”

Rubio’s remarks followed President Trump’s statement on Monday that the United States was seeing progress towards ending the conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28.

“We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected,” Trump wrote on social media after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdu-lrahman Al Thani at the White House.

The US president said further strikes were “quite unlikely”, although he maintained that Washington was “locked and loaded” if necessary.

Meanwhile, Qatar’s prime minister joined discussions with the foreign ministers of Britain, Germany, Italy, France and Saudi Arabia on the sidelines of the G7 meeting in Paris on Tuesday.

The talks, convened by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, focused on the Iran crisis and its security and economic repercussions for the region and the wider international community.

European diplomats have been urging Washington to avoid another military escalation and help restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Three tankers burning

Despite the diplomatic activity, vessels continued to come under attack in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that three oil tankers were on fire in the waterway, although they did not identify the vessels or provide details of the incidents.

The Emirati state oil company ADNOC said on Tuesday that one of its vessels had “sustained damage following an attack in the UAE’s territorial waters”, while the British maritime agency UKMTO reported a tanker was “struck by an unknown projectile” off the Omani coast.

Meanwhile, the number of loaded liquefied natural gas (LNG) tankers exiting the Strait of Hormuz reached its highest monthly level since the war began, according to vessel-tracking data released on Tuesday.

Data from S&P Global Energy showed that 31 laden LNG tankers passed through the waterway in October, up from 23 in September.

Of the October total, 23 vessels had loaded at Qatar’s Ras Laffan export terminal and eight at Das Island in the United Arab Emirates.

Separately, ship-tracking firm Kpler reported that 42 LNG cargoes were loaded in October, compared with 27 in September.

One vessel, Al Mafyar, transferred LNG to Shandong Redwood and Ejnan, both of which delivered the cargoes to Pakistan.

news.title: Microsoft presses Trump to scuttle ban on Chinese data center tech
news.text: WASHINGTON - Microsoft and other companies and trade groups have pressed the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump to halt plans to bar imports from China of a key component used in artificial intelligence data centers, three people familiar with the situation said.In August, the Trump administration was reported to be seeking a ban on U.S. imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within data centers. The concern is that they could be used by Beijing to steal data, install malware or disrupt service at U.S. data centers.Microsoft has 35 data centers under construction in the U.S. and another 134 planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company that tracks data center development. It is one of a group of companies and trade groups making the case to the Trump administration that such a ban could irreparably damage the U.S. edge over China in the AI race by further slowing the data center rollout, the sources said.

news.title: Anti-racists counter protest far-right ‘Australia Marches’ rally
news.text:
About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall on November 8. It was organised by the Refugee Action Collective Sydney (RAC) to counter the far-right Australian Marches rally against migration. 

The far-right rally, which featured speakers from One Nation, Libertarian MP John Ruddick and other right-wing influencers, rallied at the Royal Botanic Garden and drew about 500 people. 

Speakers at the counter-protest included Lynda-June Coe, Wiradjuri and Badu Island woman and NSW Greens upper house candidate; Nour Salman from Australia Palestine Advocacy Network; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Bidjigal/Gweagal activist Jordan Ryan-Hennessy; Ann El Khoury, from University of Sydney Staff for Palestine; Beau Lyon from Action for Public Housing’ and Anisa, a Somali refugee who was held in the Naoero detention centre.

Chakrabarty spoke about the racism faced by Indian migrants and linked One Nation and the Australia Marches rally to the far-right Narendra Modi government in India. 

Ian Rintoul from RAC, who chaired the rally, said the United States midterm elections were a huge blow to the racist politics of US President Donald Trump, but said anti-racist campaigners still need to get organised. 

“The tragedy is that the racist policies of Australia Marches and One Nation are being fueled by anti-migration and anti-refugee policies of the Labor government,” Rintoul said. 

“Labor is linking migration with the housing crisis; cutting the numbers of international students; has introduced fees that will make it harder for refugees to seek asylum in Australia and is implementing an ICE-like compliance force to round up people on temporary visas.”

Lyon said those in power are pushing racism to distract from the real cause of the housing crisis, the for-profit housing system. 

“Migrants are not responsible for the housing or cost of living crisis,” Rintoul said.
news.summary: About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall to counter the far-right “Australia Marches” rally against migration. Rachel Evans reports.

news.text:
BEIJING: Oil prices rose on Wednesday after falling to two-month lows in the previous session, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the Iran ​war and concerns about ongoing attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent ‌futures climbed 71 cents, or 0.78%, to $92.20 a barrel by 0119 GMT.

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 49 cents, or 0.57%, to $86.53.

New data showed that 37 ships were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and ​surrounding waterways in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, ​according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

And 10 attacks ⁠have been recorded so far in November.

Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified ​by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman, one of three ​tankers hit on Sunday for using “unauthorised routes” through the strait, according to the Iranian state broadcaster.

Another tanker was struck northeast of Oman’s Lima, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday. Iran’s Revolutionary ​Guards Navy said in a separate statement on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after ​hitting naval mines on the “unauthorized route” in the strait.

“Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase ‌in ⁠flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk,” LSEG analysts said in a November 10 note. “Meanwhile, attacks have not slowed.”

In the previous session, oil prices initially fell by more than $3 a ​barrel after US officials downplayed ​the need for further ⁠military strikes against Iran, but then gained back some of those losses after an Iranian security official said no talks were taking place between ​the two sides.

US crude oil stocks rose in the latest week, market ​sources said, ⁠citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks rose by 9 million barrels in the week ended November 6, the sources said.

In Russia, oil refining capacity has been reduced by about 30% since ⁠late ​October following renewed Ukrainian drone attacks, industry sources said.

Russian and ​Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February as US President Donald Trump’s ​envoys launched a fresh push to end the war.

news.title: Judge lets Trump's $10 billion defamation claim against BBC proceed
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC can proceed over its editing of his Jan. 6, 2021, speech, a federal judge in Miami ruled Tuesday.

U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz, whom Trump appointed, rejected the BBC’s bid to dismiss the defamation count. He dismissed a separate claim under Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act because he found the documentary was not commercial speech.

The case centers on a BBC Panorama documentary that combined portions of Trump’s speech at the Ellipse as the Capitol riot was getting under way. The 12-second clip brought together remarks separated by nearly 55 minutes. The broadcast came a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Kuntz found Trump’s complaint plausibly alleged actual malice by the BBC, the standard a public figure must satisfy to win a defamation suit. The judge wrote that the edit itself could make that allegation plausible.

“This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech,” Kuntz wrote.

The BBC characterized the cut as “ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds,” according to Kuntz’s ruling. The judge wrote that he was “not persuaded.”

Kuntz wrote that the BBC had acknowledged releasing the documentary “only a week before the 2024 Presidential Election, at the time it would have the most impact.”

Trump called the ruling a “huge victory” on Truth Social Tuesday. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” he wrote.

“We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage,” a BBC spokesperson said. The spokesperson said the BBC remained confident in its position and would continue responding through the legal process.

Trump’s lawsuit accuses the BBC of “intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring” his speech. His lawyers have described the broadcast as a “brazen” attempt to interfere in the 2024 election, an accusation the BBC denies.

The BBC previously apologized, calling the edit an “error of judgment” and saying it created “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action.” It did not offer damages. The BBC argued in its dismissal motion that the program did not meet the legal test for defamation and was unavailable in the United States.

Kuntz repeatedly noted that the BBC’s apology preceded the lawsuit, Politico reported.

The BBC argued that the court lacked personal jurisdiction because the documentary had not aired in Florida, where Trump filed the case, but Kuntz rejected that argument. He wrote that the BBC “even emailed U.S. and Florida based commenters with instructions” for viewing it.

The parties disagree over the program’s availability and viewership in the United States. Trump’s suit alleges that “hundreds of individuals” used a VPN to stream it on iPlayer in the U.S., despite an American geoblock. Earlier this year, his lawyers conceded they had no evidence it was available through BritBox, the BBC’s website, BBC Select or U.S. broadcasters.

Trump agreed to remove BBC Studios, the BBC’s commercial arm, from the suit after the broadcaster argued that it had played no part in making the documentary.

Charles Sandman, a fierce defender of Richard Nixon who opposed his impeachment, lost his seat by 16 points to Democrat Bill Hughes in the Democratic wave that followed Watergate."
