news.title: How the Hegseth Impeachment Almost Came Together—and Then Fell Completely Apart
news.text:
On Monday afternoon, Kentucky GOP Rep. Thomas Massie seemed like he could almost taste it. He had just filed his impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for a second time. The first time, in September, had prompted Republican leaders to send members home until after the election. This time, he would be able to force a vote on it within the next two days. He argued to reporters that the timing felt for success felt right: All Democrats were on board, and dozens of House Republicans who’d just lost their races had nothing to lose. Massie mocked news that Hegseth was planning to address the press to stave off the impeachment, telling reporters that he hoped Hegseth would address “the eight articles, and doesn’t get up and misquote the Bible in Quentin Tarantino fashion and do some pull-ups and call everybody fat and gay for being for this impeachment.”

When a reporter asked if any other Republicans had committed to him that they would vote for this, though, his answer was simple: “No.”

“A lot of them tell me they don’t like Hegseth,” he added after a pause, before moving on to the next question.

That dislike was worth exactly zero Republican votes late Tuesday afternoon. By a 211 to 204 vote, the House voted to refer the impeachment to committee—i.e., to kill it—with Massie remaining the lone Republican opponent. He joined all voting Democrats in that position, though 11 Democrats did not cast a vote. (Those 11 Democrats are likely to get an earful in the coming days.)

These were not the vibes heading into the week as this vote loomed. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz described Hegseth’s impeachment this week as “extremely likely” unless the secretary resigned first. House Republican leaders were acknowledging that they might lose, relying on the Senate to either dismiss the charges before a trial or at the conclusion of it. Senate Republicans were prepared to receive the articles, with several retiring senators—Thom Tillis, Joni Ernst, Bill Cassidy—even speculating that they were eager to entertain them. House Republicans were nervous about their attendance given the high levels of senioritis on their side, and the many members who blamed their loss on the Iran War that Hegseth has managed. In the end, though, only 7 Republicans missed the impeachment vote—fewer absences than the Democrats had, even though angry, despondent Republicans had good reason to let it all burn down.

Why couldn’t Massie lure any of his own to the dark side? The problems may have been Massie, himself, as well as the articles that he wrote.

Massie is a longtime irritant of his fellow House Republican members, as well as the president. A quirky libertarian, Massie was defeated by a Trump-backed primary challenger earlier this year after repeatedly casting votes against his party on issues ranging from spending to foreign policy to the release of the Epstein files. He’s not indicative of where other House Republicans are.

That showed in his impeachment resolution. What were his eight articles? Several were about how Hegseth has violated the War Powers Resolution. Others charged Hegseth with ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, authorizing extrajudicial killings against alleged drug smuggler, using DOD to retaliate against a sitting senator (Sen. Mark Kelly) for free speech, illegally capturing Venezuelan foreign leader Nicolás Maduro, and waging unauthorized war in Yemen.

Why, you might be asking, isn’t Massie directing these charges towards the guy who signs off on them—President Donald Trump?

“I think the president needs to see—this is a metaphor—one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he will see things differently,” Massie told reporters Monday. “I think politically, it’s an impossible hurdle, but also I think this is the better target. Sometimes you apply the ordnance where the best target is, and the best target is Pete Hegseth.”

Hegseth may have been the ripest political target for impeachment. But these articles weren’t written to maximize votes. Most Republicans have issues with Hegseth—his management of the Pentagon, his demotion of generals, whether he’s been accurately relaying information about the war to the president, his apparent discovery of the importance of the Strait of Hormuz only after hostilities began. They don’t have a problem with what Hegseth has done in Venezuela, or Yemen, or to people in the Caribbean, or his creative interpretations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. Most of them support most of that. And even though many don’t like that they lost their elections over high gas and other input prices sparked by the Iran War, they’re not outright opposed to confronting Iran. Massie wasn’t merely asking them to impeach Hegseth, he was asking them to reject the foreign policy of Trump’s first two years. They weren’t about to take that leap on either the policy or the politics.

Even retiring members.

“I’m not a fan of the secretary,” retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a moderate, internationalist Republican told reporters Tuesday. “But if you read the impeachment—and it’s written by Mr. Massie, who’s anti-Iran, anti-Ukraine, anti-Israel—I just don’t really align with the impeachment itself. But, surely, if you had put in about firing 80 generals and not spending appropriated money, I’d feel a little differently about it.”

Hegseth had put his own work into saving his hide. At a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning, the first such occasion in six months, Hegseth gave a speech defending his record and castigating Massie. That defense was directed less towards House Republicans, themselves, than towards the audience of one in the White House.

The most telling moment in Hegseth’s prepared remarks, as he described how “we’ve seen this show before,” was when he noted that “they” had “impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call.” That’s Trump’s specific phrasing for the 2019 call in which he pressured newly elected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to dig up dirt on the Bidens in exchange for military assistance, which led to Trump’s first impeachment. Hegseth then observed that “they impeached him again in his final week in office” (reason omitted.)

“Now, they’re trying a third time, this time against a member of his cabinet,” he continued. “They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.”

The speech went on much like this—Trump’s great, the military is doing great because of Trump, and Trump’s great—and earned its desired review in a Trump post: “Pete Hegseth gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

In other words, Trump gave the signal: He would stick by his man, for now, and Republicans had better too. If this was a test of Trump’s strength with House Republicans, even after his presidency had just brought them to their lowest point in decades, this impeachment effort didn’t put up much of a fight.
news.summary: Republicans refused to break with Donald Trump—and Democrats failed an attendance test.

news.text: President Donald Trump has issued a statement after a federal judge ruled that his lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, partially denying the British national broadcaster's motion to dmiss the case. Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz made the ruling on Tuesday that the president's $10bn (£7.5 billion) defamation lawsuit can continue. Trump is seeking substantial damages in a Florida court over the editing of a 2024 Panorama documentary about the US Capitol riots. The documentary faced criticism for giving the impression Trump had encouraged his supporters to storm the Capitol building on January 6 2021 after he lost the 2020 White House race to Joe Biden. The BBC had been seeking to have the case thrown out, warning of the “chilling effect” it would have on “robust reporting on public figures and events”. In a statement made on Truth Social, the president took to social media to hail the decision, saying: "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida. "In his powerful ruling, Judge Kuntz wrote, “Here, the news entity created the story. BBC admitted as much by confirming it had edited a video to make it appear as though President Trump made a statement he never made.” "We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP" A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process. It would be inappropriate to comment further while proceedings are ongoing.” The allegations against the documentary led the then-BBC director-general Tim Davie to announce his resignation. BBC chairman Samir Shah apologised on behalf of the broadcaster over an “error of judgment” and accepted the editing of the programme gave “the impression of a direct call for violent action”. The Trump-appointed Florida district court judge, Jeffrey T Kuntz, wrote in his ruling: “Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.” The ruling did not decide whether Mr Trump’s claims were proven. news.title: China's trade surplus soars past $1 trillion as AI boom powers exports
news.text:
BEIJING - China's trade surplus surged past $1 trillion in the first 10 months as a global race to build AI infrastructure buoyed sales of high-tech products and helped offset weak domestic demand, a dynamic likely to sharpen tensions with major trading partners.

The data comes ahead of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet for the third time this year, putting broader economic ties and tariff policy squarely in focus.

The figures highlight Beijing's growing reliance on overseas demand to support an economy hobbled by subdued consumption and a protracted property slump. But while the global AI investment boom is expected to keep demand for Chinese technology products strong into 2027, analysts warn that deeper dependence on external markets could leave China more vulnerable to protectionist measures abroad while masking persistent weakness at home.

Exports rose sharply by 35.2% in October from the same month last year in US dollar terms, customs data showed on Tuesday, only a touch slower than the 36.3% surge in September and comfortably ahead of economists' forecast for an increase of 33.5%.

That helped lift China's trade surplus to $1.04 trillion in the first 10 months, topping $1 trillion for a second consecutive year and reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.

The swelling surplus could fuel further tensions with the European Union, where leaders have called for more trade curbs with China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc over the next few years. Because the measures have yet to take effect, factories are expected to bring forward shipments, bolstering exports in the near term.

"The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets," said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.

China's trade surplus with the US narrowed slightly to $32.71 billion in October from $34.01 billion the previous month, though the broader imbalance remains a source of friction between the world's two largest economies.

Beijing and Washington on Monday formally extended by two months a trade truce that had been due to expire on Tuesday. China said last week that any expansion of purchases of US farm goods would hinge on the implementation of agreed reciprocal tariff reductions.

Imports rose 41.6% in October from a year earlier, beating the 32% increase forecast in the Reuters poll and accelerating from the 31% growth in September. Customs data also showed rare-earth exports edged higher from the previous month, while crude oil imports climbed to their highest level since March as buyers adjusted to supply disruptions in the Middle East.

"The contraction in rare-earth export volumes eased last month, suggesting that China may have begun to relax enforcement of some export controls," said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics. "This may reflect continued pressure from the US on Beijing to improve rare-earth supplies."

The data elicited little market response, with China's blue-chip CSI300 Index and the Shanghai Composite Index both edging up 0.1% by the lunch break.

One big worry for Beijing is that consumers remain reluctant to spend, constrained by a property market downturn that has battered household wealth and dented confidence in the economic outlook.

Sluggish demand at home has pushed Chinese automakers to seek sales in overseas markets. China's car exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded a 12th straight month of declines, separate data released by an industry association showed.

Greater reliance on exports, however, leaves China's economy increasingly exposed to any slowdown in global demand, with some analysts cautioning that shipment growth could cool once the AI investment cycle matures.

For now, most industry observers expect AI-related demand to remain robust. China's exports of semiconductors surged 111.1% year-on-year in the first 10 months in US dollar value terms, while overall shipments of high-tech products jumped 47.9%.

"We may see trade growth moderate next year, given the base effect," said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING.

"But AI-related trade is expected to remain strong in the months ahead despite recent equity market volatility."

news.title: Trump Aide Emerges as Dark-Horse Press Secretary Contender Despite White House Clashes
news.text:
Donald Trump is being encouraged to consider former campaign aide Caroline Sunshine for the White House press secretary role, despite former colleagues describing her previous stint in his orbit as turbulent.

Sunshine reportedly broke down in tears several times while working on Trump’s 2024 campaign, at points disappearing for hours and shutting herself in her office—occasionally alongside her boyfriend. Former colleagues told Our News Outlet that she was not offered a position in the administration after Trump returned to the White House.

The 31-year-old has now surfaced as an unexpected contender to succeed Katie Zacharia, whose time as press secretary lasted only five days after she took over from Karoline Leavitt.

Bill Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and a prominent Trump ally, reportedly promoted Sunshine’s candidacy during dinner with the president at Mar-a-Lago last weekend, according to a source close to Trump.

The dinner followed Sunshine’s appearance on Fox News, where she called for chief of staff Susie Wiles to resign. Her comments came less than a day before Wiles’s sudden departure.

One former colleague recalled Sunshine’s earlier period working for Trump this way: ‘Breakdowns in the bathroom, breakdowns in her office, kind of walking around the office with mascara running down her face. Something was obviously wrong, but no one really knew what it was or what was happening.’

The open position has prompted a behind-the-scenes lobbying effort at Mar-a-Lago, with much of the advocacy being conducted through intermediaries, the source close to the president said.

Sunshine was not present at Trump’s Florida club over the weekend, but Pulte reportedly mentioned her to Trump, Stephen Miller—who has replaced Wiles as chief of staff—and others.

‘You know who would be really good as press secretary? Caroline Sunshine,’ Pulte allegedly told the president.

Trump is said to have replied: ‘You think so? She does a good job on television, but she says bad things about me. She’s been doing better lately.’

Trump then sought Miller’s view, with the chief of staff responding: ‘Yeah, she’s been doing good on TV recently.’

Privately, however, Miller has a far less favorable opinion of Sunshine, according to the source. ‘Stephen hates her. Whenever her name comes up in the Oval, he piles on,’ the source said.

Miller replaced Wiles as chief of staff on Monday. He has been contacted for comment.

According to the source, Sunshine has been pursuing the role remotely by using allies who have access to Trump. ‘She keeps trying to find people to bring her up. It’s a full-court press,’ the source said.

At the same time, Sunshine spent months criticizing Trump’s handling of the war in Iran, including during appearances on CNN.

Her criticism reached a peak last Wednesday on Fox News’s ‘Jesse Watters Primetime,’ where she directly called for Wiles to step down.

‘Susie Wiles needs to resign,’ Sunshine told host Jesse Watters. ‘She needs to offer her resignation to the president before he has to ask for it.’

‘I think it was a dumb move on her part. I don’t understand what her end game is,’ a source said.

Sunshine had previously defended Trump after the election, telling Fox: ‘Tonight was not a failure for the president. Tonight was his base saying, “We still like you, we just don’t like the direction that you’re taking us in.”‘

A former Disney Channel performer, Sunshine appeared in the 2010 sitcom Shake It Up. She later served as a press assistant in Trump’s first administration and became press secretary for Vivek Ramaswamy’s presidential campaign.

She joined Trump’s 2024 campaign as deputy communications director at its headquarters in downtown West Palm Beach, Florida.

Former colleagues said her visible distress became a concern. One said they personally saw Sunshine crying ‘at least two to three’ times, including in the bathroom and inside her office.

When staff members checked on her, they asked whether the problem was connected to her personal life or her work. The source said Sunshine declined to discuss it.

Her boyfriend at the time, Jack Advent, 23, was the producer responsible for Trump’s campaign TikTok videos. Trump nicknamed him ‘TikTok Jack.’ When Advent was back in West Palm Beach, he reportedly spent hours in Sunshine’s office, the source said.

Advent spent much of the campaign traveling with Trump to film the president, and colleagues praised the results of his work. ‘He produced good metrics that people were happy with,’ one said.

Sources said Sunshine locked her office door for extended periods on several occasions, sometimes while Advent was with her, at times when colleagues believed she should have been working.

‘I’d love to know what she was up to. I can’t say I know because the door was locked,’ one former colleague said.

Those who mentioned the locked office emphasized that they never saw or heard anything inappropriate between Sunshine and Advent.

Another source remembered a day when Sunshine did not appear to be in the office, only for colleagues to see her on television.

‘I remember sitting in the office and not seeing her at all that day, wondering where she was and why she wasn’t helping with incoming,’ the source said.

The colleague who saw Sunshine crying said she appeared to work according to her own timetable. She could seem diligent one day, the source said, then be absent for three hours at a time the next.

Sunshine was brought in to respond to press inquiries under Leavitt, who was then the campaign’s national press secretary. However, two former colleagues said she appeared more interested in television appearances.

‘She was interested in being on TV and getting public attention. She was not interested in what she was hired to do,’ one source said.

Another former colleague described her as ‘lazy’ and said: ‘She didn’t have her priorities straight. She wasn’t doing what she was hired to do.’

Former colleagues said Sunshine was eventually taken off press-inquiry duties and spent the final weeks of the campaign escorting reporters up and down the steps of the press plane.

Five former colleagues said Sunshine was not offered a role in the administration after the campaign concluded.

Sunshine, Pulte and the White House declined to comment. Advent did not respond to requests for comment.

news.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Hegseth
news.text:
Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, winning a reprieve for the polarising Pentagon chief before Democrats take control of Congress next year and possibly try again.

The vote on a procedural motion came just hours after Hegseth blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce and delivered a defiant defence of his record at the helm of the US military, winning praise from US President Donald Trump.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favour of a motion to refer eight articles of impeachment to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, a move that the sponsor of the impeachment push, US Representative Thomas Massie, warned would kill it.

Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, had hoped to draw votes from Republicans upset with Hegseth’s policies and wary of the unpopularity of the war on Iran, but no other Republicans joined him.

Democrats had voiced strong support for the impeachment effort. But 11 Democrats, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, did not vote.

If eight of them had, the procedural measure would have been defeated, paving the way for a full House impeachment vote. Pelosi’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on why she missed the vote.

Trump cheered the results in a social media post, saying the effort to impeach Hegseth “has miserably FAILED!”

In a sign that the impeachment episode may have drawn Trump and Hegseth closer together, Trump added that Hegseth’s performance on Iran, Venezuela and other issues “led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

Hegseth would have been the first US defence secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title “secretary of war”.

Hegseth calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when he took office last year. Trump cannot change the name of the Defence Department without approval from Congress.

Iran war anger

Voter anger over the war on Iran, which has settled into an effective stalemate focused on securing the Strait of Hormuz, helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress, which takes office in January, to act to end the war once and for all.

Although Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war and blamed it for the Republicans’ midterm rout, he voiced support for Hegseth on Tuesday.

“This isn’t about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon,” Vance wrote on social media.

Before the vote, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday: “Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran.”

Hegseth has repeatedly defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran’s military has been left in ruins. He also said his orders to US forces were lawful, despite Massie’s accusations of “high crimes and misdemeanours” ranging from the war itself to the US military raid in January to depose Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

“History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now,” Hegseth said on Tuesday at his first Pentagon briefing in six months.

Jeffries said he would talk to members about whether to mount a new impeachment effort in the next Congress. “We’ll have that conversation at the appropriate time,” he said.

A Democratic-led push to impeach Hegseth could be far more intense, with lawmakers calling in top brass to testify, including generals and admirals fired by Hegseth who have remained silent so far. Hegseth, who has railed against diversity efforts at the Pentagon, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who is Black, and the Navy’s top admiral, a woman, among others.

In such an effort, Democrats could also raise other issues concerning to voters including Pentagon policy toward Ukraine and the US military’s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Caribbean and Pacific waters.

Some Republicans say Hegseth’s strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in the military’s budget to $1.5 trillion from $950 billion.

Massie said he was disappointed by the vote, comparing Republicans to passengers content to go down with the Titanic.

“They know it’s a sinking ship but committed to stay on board,” he said.

news.title: Kennedy family asks court to block Trump's 250-foot arch near Arlington
news.text:
Nine Kennedy family members asked a federal court Tuesday to block President Donald Trump’s planned 250-foot arch, saying it would cast shadows over relatives’ graves at Arlington National Cemetery.

The relatives argue in their filing that the arch would obstruct views from Arlington Memorial Bridge to the family’s gravesites, including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame. They say it would block “a line of sight that was designed to represent the unification of the Nation following the Civil War and that has existed for nearly a century.”

When they visit, family members “pray and reflect upon the relationship between the Lincoln Memorial, the Kennedy Gravesites, and the Eternal Flame, finding solace in seeing the legacy of the Kennedy family memorialized spatially,” according to the filing.

Speaking for the family, Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said “a towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles” would “also cast a shadow over our democratic principles.”

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said it was “unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery.”

Commission vote and court order

The family’s motion follows a suit Washington, D.C., and Virginia brought against the National Park Service and Interior Department in late October. The jurisdictions called the arch flagrantly unlawful, saying Trump had not sought approval from Congress.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an October filing that the arch could serve as “a dual-purpose structure: a major national monument that also incorporates military utility to support Homeland defense.”

The National Capital Planning Commission approved the plans by an 8-4 vote following a nine-hour meeting that drew more than 100 public remarks, most opposing the arch.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan then barred construction-related activity on the arch in a 14-day temporary restraining order issued last week. In a statement last week, Ingle described the arch as “a tribute to 250 years of American greatness.”

In an emailed statement to The Hill, Ingle said “an activist district court has temporarily blocked the construction of the long-awaited Arch.”

The relatives filed Tuesday’s motion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. They want the court to prevent any approval, authorization or construction of the arch unless Congress authorizes it and designates a sponsor, and all statutory requirements are met.

Norman Eisen and Steve Jonas of Democracy Defenders Fund, the family’s lawyers, said “only Congress has the constitutional power to authorize an intrusion of this magnitude.”

Earlier Kennedy Center dispute

Joe Kennedy III wrote on X on Dec. 18, 2025, that the Kennedy Center “can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.”

The Kennedy Center is a living memorial to a fallen president and named for President Kennedy by federal law. It can no sooner be renamed than can someone rename the Lincoln Memorial, no matter what anyone says.— Joe Kennedy III (@joekennedy) December 18, 2025

He and Kerry Kennedy opposed Trump’s attempts to put his name on the center, where it appeared on the facade before later being removed. Both joined Tuesday’s motion as part of the group of nine relatives.

The plaintiffs include children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, who were brothers of President John F. Kennedy. The three brothers are buried at Arlington.

The administration says the arch would mark 250 years of American independence, and it would stand on a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. Trump has previously said he intends to complete it before leaving office in two years.

An administration review released by the National Park Service in August acknowledged that the arch would adversely affect as many as 42 historic sites. The government has argued in court that the project is lawful and that the plaintiffs lack standing to sue.

Opponents say the structure would interrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House and disturb the solemnity of funerals at Arlington, CNN reported. The outlet said the legal challenges have complicated Trump’s goal of finishing the arch before he leaves office.

University of Connecticut history professor Micki McElya discussed the arch’s potential negative effects on Arlington National Cemetery on a Bloomberg Law podcast. “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation,” Ingle said. “We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”

The plaintiffs have requested a longer-term injunction. Chutkan’s 14-day order expires unless extended.
news.summary: Nine relatives say the planned arch would obstruct views of family gravesites, including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame.

news.title: ‘Trump did nothing’: Chuck Schumer questions president’s silence after Nvidia CEO spy briefing, shares plun...
news.text:
Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has accused US President Donald Trump of failing to protect national security after reports emerged that the president had been briefed about Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, but took no action.
In a post on X, Schumer said Trump ignored the intelligence briefing and continued engaging with Huang, while backing US chip access for China.
Trump was briefed over A YEAR AGO on Nvidia’s CEO having an affair with a Chinese spy. He did nothing about it.
Instead, Trump took him to Beijing, took his advice to give China access to our AI chips, & accepted a $25M donation from Nvidia.
We need answers immediately on Trump’s failure to protect our national security
— Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) November 10, 2026
"Trump was briefed over A YEAR AGO on Nvidia’s CEO having an affair with a Chinese spy. He did nothing about it. Instead, Trump took him to Beijing, took his advice to give China access to our AI chips, & accepted a $25M donation from Nvidia. We need answers immediately on Trump’s failure to protect our national security," Schumer wrote.
The remarks came after a report by The New York Times revealed that Trump was briefed about the intelligence concerning Huang while aboard Air Force One in May, as he travelled to China for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Rubio briefed Trump aboard Air Force One
A New York Times report confirmed that Rubio briefed Trump after learning that Huang would be joining the trip, he said intelligence had obtained sensitive information suggesting Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be working for China's Ministry of State Security.
The briefing took place shortly before Huang joined the presidential delegation travelling to Beijing. Trump had initially left the Nvidia chief off the invitation list but later invited him to join Air Force One during a refuelling stop in Alaska.
However, Trump was reportedly unmoved by the information and proceeded with his plan to bring the Nvidia chief to China.
The latest disclosure contradicts Trump's remarks on Monday, when he denied knowing about Huang's relationship with the woman, identified as Alice Huang, at the time of his May visit to China.
"No, I didn't hear about it then," Trump said in a press conference, when asked whether he knew about the relationship before travelling to meet Xi.
When questioned about whether he had received an intelligence briefing on the matter last year, Trump said he would have to check with intelligence officials, adding that the information had not made much of an impact on him.
Trump defends Nvidia chief
Despite the allegations, Trump has continued to defend Huang, describing him as an "honourable man".
The president said he had spoken to the Nvidia chief and asked whether he knew that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. According to Trump, Jensen Huang said he was unaware of her intelligence links.
Trump also said he did not intend to raise the matter with Xi during his upcoming visit to China next week.
The president had initially suggested that Huang could accompany him on the trip but confirmed on Monday that the Nvidia chief would not be part of the delegation.
The New York Times report also said Rubio had overseen the preparation of a memorandum about Huang in the weeks before the May visit. The document was circulated among a small group of senior administration officials but was not intended for Trump and was not shown to him aboard Air Force One.
Nvidia shares tumble, Microsoft overtakes chipmaker
Meanwhile, Nvidia's shares fell more than 6 per cent on Tuesday amid uncertainty surrounding the company's outlook for artificial intelligence and the investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.
The decline pushed Nvidia below Microsoft in market valuation, making the latter the world's second-most valuable company.
Microsoft shares were down 0.4 per cent at $543.25, while Nvidia lost more than 6 per cent to trade at around $167.11.
The controversy has intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's position in the US-China technology rivalry. The company is a critical supplier of advanced chips used to power artificial intelligence systems, making its technology central to Washington's efforts to maintain an advantage over Beijing.
The US began restricting direct sales of advanced chips to China in late 2022. However, Chinese companies have continued to access computing power through data centres in Southeast Asia, including facilities operated by Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company where Alice Huang previously held an executive position.
Following the New York Times' earlier report last month, Nvidia executives and Huang initially described their association with the woman as a routine business engagement with a customer.
However, Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with her on Sunday. Nvidia subsequently announced that it would conduct an independent investigation into the matter.
The company said its board had no reason to believe that its trade secrets or national security had been compromised and that a committee of independent directors would oversee the investigation.

news.title: India garment makers rethink reliance on US after tariff shock
news.text:
ReutersIn April to August, India's textile, apparel and home-furnishings exports to the US fell 9.8% to $4.0 billion, while shipments to other markets rose 3.7% to $15.2 billion.

RANCHI: At Orient Craft's factory in Ranchi, hundreds of women stitch dresses, shirts and children's clothing for British retailers Next and Marks & Spencer.Not long ago, most of Orient Craft's output would have gone to the US. But founder Sudhir Dhingra, 77, has cut shipments there since the US hiked tariffs, which rose to as much as 50% last year, hitting orders from customers including American Eagle and Gap.Also read | Zara owner Inditex commits $50 million to fund low-cost loans for suppliers going greenEven with duties now lower and the possibility of a trade pact, Dhingra has decided it is too much of a risk to depend so heavily on one market."Even if there is a deal, what is the guarantee that it will hold water?" he said. "I don't wish to see that sword on my head."Live EventsOrient Craft is one of many Indian companies reconfiguring their export destinations, and their exposure to the US, in light of the tariff shock, in a move that is likely to strengthen New Delhi's hand in its trade negotiations with Washington, and potentially reduce India's vulnerability to US pressure over time.Dhingra said US buyers cancelled orders or sought discounts after US President Donald Trump first announced the tariff hikes in April 2025, with some asking suppliers to absorb 25% of the duty, despite manufacturers' margins being less than 10%.Orient Craft has since moved sales to Britain, Europe and, to a lesser extent, India. The US now accounts for less than 10% of sales, down from 84% before the tariffs, with annual exports of about 1.5 billion rupees ($15.82 million).US duties on Indian products are currently 10% under Section 301, a US law allowing tariffs on imports, as well as base tariffs from 6% to 12%.Gokaldas Exports, which employs more than 53,000 people and is one of India's biggest garment exporters, is turning to Europe.Also read | India's apparel production falls 5.6% in H1 FY27 as weak US demand, high costs hit manufacturers"It is not a temporary shift," said Managing Director Sivaramkrishnan Ganapathi.The company aims to raise Europe's revenue share to 25% to 30% over the next 3 to 5 years, he said, from 15% to 16%, reducing the US share to 35% to 40% from 50% to 55%.In April to August, India's textile, apparel and home-furnishings exports to the US fell 9.8% to $4.0 billion, while shipments to other markets rose 3.7% to $15.2 billion, according to the Global Trade Research Institute.The US share of Indian exports fell to 25.4% at the end of August from 28.3% in 2022, according to industry estimates.BUILDING NEW MARKETS, LOWERING COSTSExporters said US tariff uncertainty, higher shipping costs and US buyers' discount demands have squeezed margins, making other markets, including the UAE, UK and EU, look more attractive.Indian clothing also gets duty-free access to Britain under the India-UK trade deal that came into effect in July, while a similar EU agreement could eliminate duties of 12% to 17%."Germany, France, Italy and the Netherlands are key targets," said A. Sakthivel, chairman of the Apparel Export Promotion Council, an industry group.Exporters are also looking to lower manufacturing costs.Ranchi, in the eastern state of Jharkhand, is best known for coal and iron ore, but is now luring garment factories with subsidies, easier land access and its educated and reliable workforce.Reuters visited three factories in and around Ranchi, together employing about 8,000 people."We have at least a 10% efficiency advantage here over other locations," said Mrityunjay Singh, senior vice president of operations at Gokaldas, which has two factories in Ranchi and plans to open a third, creating up to 4,600 jobs."We can't rely on a single market, product or buyer," said Birendra Rawat of Ranchi-based Auburn Design, which makes Jockey underwear and clothing for local licensee Page Industries , and produces 5 million to 6 million garments a month to be sold in India and neighbouring countries.India's own apparel market, valued at $150 billion and growing 7% to 8% annually, provides a buffer against export uncertainty through steadier cash flows and demand."Diversification is becoming a structural strategy, especially for exporters heavily exposed to the US market," said Chandrima Chatterjee, secretary general of the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry.Exporters said they would not abandon the US completely given the size of the market and longstanding relationships with buyers, but the upheaval of the tariff shock meant it was unlikely to regain its former dominance, even if duties eased."The US market remains important, but it can't decide the future of thousands of families who depend on us," Dhingra said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump and Netanyahu in ‘shouting match from hell’ during Iran call – media
news.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a heated phone call with US President Donald Trump over the possibility of renewed military strikes against Iran, Ynet reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the conversation.

Several media outlets, including Axios, the Associated Press and the Financial Times, previously reported that Netanyahu had been urging Trump to resume military operations against Iran shortly after the US midterm elections. Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate in the November 3 vote, widely seen as a rebuke to Trump’s policies, including the unpopular war with Iran, which has driven up energy prices.

Ynet described the weekend conversation as unusually tense, with one source calling it a “shouting match from hell.” Netanyahu’s office dismissed the report as “fake news, absolute nonsense,” while a senior Israeli official confirmed that the call took place but denied that it had been confrontational.

Trump said on Sunday that he saw no reason to escalate the conflict with Iran, amid opposition to renewed strikes from Washington’s Arab allies in the region. He and US Vice President J.D. Vance have acknowledged that the Iran war contributed to the Republicans’ election defeat.

Nevertheless, Trump stood by his decision to launch the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran on February 28. “I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” he told the Wall Street Journal after the vote.

Netanyahu’s political future is also uncertain after his coalition failed to secure a parliamentary majority in Israel’s October 27 elections.

On Sunday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Netanyahu’s main rival, former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, with forming a new government after parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended him for the premiership, compared with 46 who backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a governing coalition, with a possible two-week extension. 

The war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil and liquefied natural gas trade. Trump has vowed to maintain the naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has been attacking tankers using US-designated shipping routes, which Tehran considers illegal.

news.title: Kennedy family members ask a judge to block Trump’s Arlington memorial arch
news.text:
Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge Tuesday to block President Donald Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.

The shadow would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites,” the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.

The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK’s gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.

Building the arch would be a “permanent denigration” of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring “would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended,” lawyers for the relatives wrote. They are represented by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and Democracy Defenders Fund.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary who has a fractured relationship with many of his relatives, did not join the lawsuit.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.

The White House last week unveiled a glitzy new website to showcase the arch, which is slated to rise in a mass of gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

news.title: Some relief as crude slips below USD 90 for the first time since August
news.text: NEW DELHI: Giving a shot in the arm to Indian markets, international oil benchmark Brent crude fell below $90 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since August as US President Donald Trump signalled that the West Asia war may be coming to a close.Brent, the price gauge for around 80% of global crude, hit a low of $89.03 per barrel in morning trade in London.Crude oil is a big burden on India’s imports bill, with the country sourcing 85% of its requirements from overseas. Falling prices could translate into lower transport costs and lower prices of goods and services, thus improving the purchasing power of households.The fall in crude prices will likely bring cheers to equities, bonds and the rupee, and if the price sustains it may prompt RBI to rethink its pace in the battle against inflation.On Monday, the Sensex added 107.25 points, or 0.13%, to close at 81,106.65, while the Nifty50 closed 58.25 points, or 0.23%, higher at 25,044.65. On Tuesday, the markets remained closed for Diwali-Balipratipada. The rupee has weakened nearly 4% against the dollar this year, despite gaining some ground in recent weeks..Analysts, however, aren’t willing to uncork the bubbly early. They said the fall in prices may not last long as global oil supplies remain tight and countries will need to replenish their strategic reserves.“Global reserves, particularly in OECD countries and China, have come down considerably and have been drawn upon during the disruption,” said Prashant Vasisht, senior vice-President and co-group head, corporate sector, ICRA.Vasisht said countries would need to rebuild their strategic petroleum reserves.Earlier, the West Asia conflict had triggered a massive price shock with Brent soaring to a peak of $118 in March.PRICE CORRECTIONThe fall in oil prices came after US President Donald Trump said he would hold off on fresh strikes against Iran. Hopes of a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine also supported the fall in pricesIndian basket average costThe Indian crude basket averaged $100.01 a barrel in November, down 17% from $119.91 in October. It had averaged $116.09 in September, $90.19 in August and $82.04 in July. news.title: Judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
news.text:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.A judge ordered Trump last month to answer questions under oath in the lawsuit by 11 December, after the president cancelled a previous deposition last month, citing "matters of national importance".

A lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia in October on the scheduled day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Earlier this year, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally argued - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, from his defamation lawsuit, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".
news.summary: A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.
news.author: David Apinga
